opening.headline: In function calls where the model appears to query an external system directly, the round-trip flow of calls describes who is actually executing what.
body: When I asked, “Tell me what the weather is like in Seoul today,” the answer I got was, “It’s currently sunny and 22 degrees in Seoul.” Even though the model cannot know today's weather based on learned knowledge alone, on the surface it appears as if the model has directly queried an external system.

In this class, we'll explain step by step what happens behind the scenes. It distinguishes between what the tool schema tells the model, what messages are sent between call requests and results, and where the model's work and the application's work are divided.

As of 2026-10: Claude Opus 5.5·Sonnet 5.5·Fable 5.1·Mythos 5.1 rejects any/tool in tool_choice with 400 error. Use auto and strict tool input validation, but strict does not enforce the call itself. The four-value comparison below is limited to models that support forced calls.

screens.title: It looks like the model is directly querying the DB.
screens.lead:
Read the conversation below and think about the questions first. The starting point of this class is whether the apparent conversation is the same as what actually happened.

visual.alt: A scene showing a short conversation between the user and the assistant, and the external system hidden behind it, with a question mark.
labels: Please tell me the weather in Seoul today
It's currently sunny and 22 degrees in Seoul.

paragraphs: The user said, “Tell me the weather today in Seoul,” and the assistant responded, “It’s currently sunny and 22 degrees in Seoul.” Just looking at the conversation, it feels very natural. However, the model cannot know today's weather with only the learned knowledge. This is because today's weather is information that was created after learning was completed.

So where did this answer come from? On the surface, it looks like the model accessed an external system and looked up the weather directly. The impression of a model that directly queries the database is created because the dialog screen hides the intermediate steps.

In reality, there are multiple requests and responses going back and forth behind the scenes of the conversation. Knowing who sent what messages and who executed the code helps you know where to fix your tools when they don't work.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Who actually did what? By the end of the lesson, you will be able to answer this question step by step.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the confusing part of the function call.

screens.title: What is the most confusing part of a function call?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. First think about which part you were confused about and then click it. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.answer: Models do not execute functions. What the model does is ask to call a certain function with certain arguments. The app runs it. This is a key distinction in this lesson, and you'll see the rationale in the screens that follow.

items.prompt: What shape does the result return?
items.answer: The result is returned along with an identifier for which call it was made. Claude uses `tool_use_id`, and OpenAI uses `call_id`. The appearance varies from provider to provider, but the principle of grouping calls and results into identifiers is the same.

items.prompt: When does the model decide to call?
items.answer: The model looks at the user request and tooltip to determine whether to invoke it. So, if your tooltip is poor, it won't call when it's needed or will call at the wrong time. For instructions on how to write a description, see line by line in the following screen.

items.prompt: What does it mean to “call round trip”?
items.answer: This means that it doesn't end with just one request. When the app sends a question, the model returns a call request, and after the app executes it, it sends a second request with the results, and the model creates the final answer. The second request is a round trip.

screens.outro: Let's start by reading the tool schema, which introduces the tool to the model.

screens.title: Tool schema: What does each line tell the model?
screens.lead: Below is the definition of the weather lookup tool. When you select a highlighted passage, an explanation appears, explaining what that line tells the model and what symptoms occur if it is misaligned.

visual.alt: The tool definition is divided into three parts: name, description, and input structure and is passed to the model.
labels: Read the list of tools and decide whether to call them
the shape of the Son of Man

marks.note: This is the name the model uses when calling. Claude only allows up to 128 characters including letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens. If spaces are included, the format does not fit. As the number of tools increases, a namespace name prefixed with the service name, such as `github_list_prs`, makes the choice clear.

marks.span: "description": "Get the current weather in a given location"
marks.note: It's a line that tells you what the tool does and when to use it, and is the most important factor in the tool's performance. If it's too short, the model won't call it when it's needed, or it'll call it at the wrong time. In practice, it's better to write down what you do, when you use it, and what you don't do in 3-4 sentences.

Set the name and shape of the arguments the model will create. If the name is different from what your app code reads, the app will not find the argument. OpenAI contains name, description, and parameters in a tool whose type is function, and Gemini reports the same information through function declarations.

marks.span: "description": "The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA"
marks.note: This is a line that informs the value format of the argument along with an example. Without this description, the model guesses whether the format is Seoul or Seoul Metropolitan City.
Specifies required arguments. If this line is omitted, the call may be made without `location`, and the app will attempt to query with an empty value.

screens.outro: Now that you've read the definition, let's look at the round-trip flow between calls and results.

screens.title: Round trip calls: tool_use and tool_result
screens.lead: Selecting a number marker will reveal a detailed description of who is doing what at that step. Please check steps 1 to 5 in order.

visual.alt: Sequence diagram showing the five-step call round trip between the app and the model.

markers.label: Send questions and tool definitions
markers.title: App sends first request
markers.body: The app sends the tool definition in the request along with the user's question. It starts with a request containing OpenAI's flowchart tool. At this point, the model has not yet looked up the weather. The model reads the tool list and determines whether a call is needed.

markers.label: Model's call request
markers.title: The model makes a call, not an answer
markers.body: `"stop_reason": "tool_use"` in Claude's response signals that the model has stopped requesting a call rather than an answer. The response contains the following blocks: `{"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01", "name": "get_weather", "input": {"location": "Seoul"}}`. The app selects the code to execute as `name`, passes `input`, and remembers `id`.

markers.label: App executes a function
markers.title: The actual execution is done by the app.
markers.body: The app actually runs code `get_weather` to get results from the weather system. These steps answer the questions in this lesson. It is the app that is querying the external system, not the model. The app is also responsible for checking permissions and handling errors at this stage. It is safer for the app to check the range and format of the value one more time, rather than trusting the arguments created by the model as is.

markers.label: return result
markers.title: The result is sent together with the call.
markers.body: The app sends the user message in the second request with `{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01", "content": "Sunny, 22 degrees"}`. `tool_use_id` must be correct to know which call the model is the result of. OpenAI binds it to a call identifier such as `function_call_output` containing `call_id`, and Gemini returns it to the function_result stage containing `call_id`. If an error occurred during execution, it displays `"is_error": true` in Claude's `tool_result`.

markers.label: final response
markers.title: Model creates natural language answers
markers.body: The model reads the results and creates a natural language answer: “It is currently sunny and 22 degrees in Seoul.” All the user sees is this last answer. Since the intermediate call request and results were not displayed on the screen, it appeared as if the model had queried them directly.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the round trip, let's look at the difference depending on who runs the tool.

screens.title: Who Runs It: Client Tools and Server Tools
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the execution location and number of round trips change. At the end, you'll also see options for controlling the model's tool selection.

states.label: client tools
states.body: Client tools run in your app. The model should only return the call request and return a result after the app executes it. This is the case with the weather tool on the front screen. So the round trip takes at least two requests, and if the app misses the call request received in the first request, the flow stops here. The model determines whether to call by looking at the user request and the tool description. If Claude's `tool_choice` is `auto`, this decision is left to the model. If you specify that a specific tool should be used, the model returns the call directly without any explanation.

states.label: server tools
states.body: Server tools are tools like `web_search` that Anthropic runs on their infrastructure and returns the results in the same response. Since there are no steps that the app directly executes or returns results to, the round trip is a single request. The biggest difference is that the responsibility for execution lies with the provider rather than the app. However, even with server tools, the app designs which tools to open and how to use the results. Parallel calls can be turned off in Claude with `disable_parallel_tool_use`, and in OpenAI by leaving `parallel_tool_calls` false, zero or only one tool will be called.

screens.outro: Now let's move on to the analysis of dividing the work of the model and the work of the app.

screens.title: Analysis: What the model does and what the application does
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to follow the instructor's classification of each task as either a model or an app. Note that execution and responsibility are both on the app side.

data.caption: The role of the model and the role of the app in function calls
rows: Determine whether a call is needed from a user request
This is because the model reads the request and tooltip and makes decisions.
Create tool names and arguments according to the schema.
`input` or `arguments` is generated by the model according to the shape of the schema.
Receives a call and executes the actual function or API
This is because models cannot execute code, they can only make call requests.
The execution result is returned with `tool_use_id` or `call_id`.
This is because the result of which call must be bound with an identifier for the model to understand the result.
Responsible for verifying permissions, error handling, and safety of execution results.
Since the app is the one actually touching the external system, the safety responsibility also lies with the app.
data.notes: The model simply asks, “Please call this function with these arguments,” and it’s up to the app to decide whether to accept the request or how to execute it. Even if the argument matches the schema, the app must check whether the value is safe. For example, a function that deletes a file should not be executed simply because the model requested it; the app should check the target and permissions first. It is especially important in security design that execution responsibility lies with the app.

screens.outro: Now that we've divided the roles, let's read and fix one of the loose tool definitions.

screens.title: Commentary: Reading and fixing poor tool definitions
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the instructor as he finds and fixes problem lines in the tool definition, one by one. The symptom is that even if you ask "What's the weather in Seoul?", the tool is not called, or even if it is called, the argument is empty.

steps.title: Step 1 Read the definition
steps.body:
The definition of the problem is as follows.

```json
{"name": "get weather", "description": "weather",
 "input_schema": {"type": "object",
   "properties": {"loc": {"type": "string"}}}}
```

The name has a space, the description is one word, the argument name is `loc`, and there are no required specifications.

steps.title: Step 2 name line
steps.body: `get weather` contains spaces and does not fit the allowed format of letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens. Fix it to `get_weather`.

steps.title: Step 3 description line
steps.body: The single word “weather” doesn’t tell you what a tool does or when you should use it. Write 3 to 4 sentences explaining that you are looking up the current weather by city and that you are using it when asking about the weather. This line is the biggest basis for judging whether or not to call.

steps.title: Step 4 properties and required lines
steps.body: `loc` has unclear meaning and has no explanation and `required`. Change the name to `location`, add a format example like `"The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA"`, and put it in `required`.

steps.title: Step 5 Confirmation
steps.body: If you send a request with the modified definition, it returns a response with models `stop_reason` as `tool_use` and `input` as `{location: Seoul}`. If the app returns "Sunny, 22 degrees" as `tool_result` with `tool_use_id`, the model creates a natural language answer. This completes one round trip.

screens.outro: Now that I've finished editing, I'll close by summarizing the main points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Model makes request, app executes
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Find out the answer to the question we asked in the beginning: who actually did what.

paragraphs: To answer your first question, the model did not look up the weather. The model asked to call `get_weather` with the argument Seoul, and the app executed the function and returned the result. The model simply read the results and created a natural language answer. Because the conversation screen hid the intermediate steps, it looked like the model had viewed it directly.

The tool schema consists of a name, description, and parameter schema, of which the description determines the decision to call the model. Call requests and results are exchanged using identifiers such as `tool_use_id` or `call_id`. One round trip consists of a question request, a call request, execution of the app, a second request with the results, and a final response.

You can adjust the calling method with `tool_choice` and parallel calling options. Either way, the app is responsible for running the client tool, so permissions, error handling, and safety verification of results must be designed into the app.

callout.label: distinction to remember
callout.text: The model requests a call, and the app executes it. If a tool doesn't work, first check the tool description and the identifier in the results.

glossary.def: This is a definition that describes the tool's name, description, and input parameter structure in JSON Schema.
In Claude, this is the model's call request block and the result block returned by the app. They are tied together by tool_use_id.
It is a flow consisting of a request, a request to call the model, execution of the app, a second request with the result, and a final response.
The idea is to decide which tool the model will call, and control that choice with options like tool_choice.

misconceptions.myth: The model executes the function directly.
misconceptions.fact: In a client tool, the model requests a call and the app executes it. Models do not execute code.

misconceptions.myth: The call ends with a single request.
misconceptions.fact: The second request that returns the result is a round trip. If you don't return a result, the model won't produce a final answer.

misconceptions.myth: Even if you write the description roughly, the model will understand it on its own.
misconceptions.fact: Description is the most important factor in tool selection performance. You need to be specific about what you will do and when you will write it.

misconceptions.myth: The name can be whatever you want.
misconceptions.fact: Claude only accepts letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens. Prefixing the service name makes the choice clear when there are many tools.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The model requests a call and the app executes it.
The tool schema consists of a name, description, and parameter schema, with the description determining the selection.
The result is returned tied to the call by tool_use_id or call_id.
Control the calling method with tool_choice and parallel calling options.
